title: Objects, data structures and the Law of Demeter
questions:
  - id: demeter
    prompt: "Which line violates the Law of Demeter?"
    options:
      - id: train
        text: "`order.GetCustomer().GetAddress().GetCountry().TaxRate`"
        correct: true
      - text: "`order.Total()`"
      - text: "`customer.PlaceOrder(cart)`"
      - text: "`items.Where(i => i.IsActive).ToList()`"
    explanation: Reaching through several objects couples the caller to the internal structure of each. Fluent LINQ chains return new objects of the same abstraction and are not considered violations.
  - id: tell-dont-ask
    prompt: What does "tell, don't ask" encourage?
    options:
      - text: Avoiding all getters in every class
      - text: Logging every method call
      - id: tell
        text: Telling an object to perform behaviour rather than pulling its data out and deciding for it
        correct: true
    explanation: Behaviour should live next to the data it needs, which keeps invariants inside the object.
  - id: anemic
    prompt: Which statements describe an anemic domain model?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Entities are bags of public getters and setters with no behaviour
        correct: true
      - text: Business rules are scattered across service classes
        correct: true
      - text: Invariants such as "total cannot be negative" are enforced inside the entity
    explanation: In an anemic model, rules live outside the objects, so nothing prevents invalid state.
---
## Learning objectives

- Distinguish objects (behaviour, hidden data) from data structures (exposed data, no behaviour)
- Apply the Law of Demeter and "tell, don't ask"
- Recognise and fix anemic models

## Two different things

| Objects | Data structures |
|---------|-----------------|
| Hide data, expose behaviour | Expose data, have little behaviour |
| Easy to add new types | Easy to add new functions |
| `Account.Withdraw(amount)` | `record AccountDto(int Id, decimal Balance)` |

Both are useful. DTOs crossing a network boundary *should* be plain data. Domain objects that guard
business rules should hide their state.

## The Law of Demeter

A method should only talk to its immediate friends: its own fields, its parameters, objects it
creates, and its own methods.

```csharp
// Train wreck
var rate = order.GetCustomer().GetAddress().GetCountry().TaxRate;

// Ask the object that knows
var taxRate = order.TaxRate();
```

## Tell, don't ask

```csharp
// Asking — the rule lives outside the object
if (account.Balance >= amount)
{
    account.Balance -= amount;
}

// Telling — the object protects its own invariant
account.Withdraw(amount);

public sealed class Account
{
    public decimal Balance { get; private set; }

    public void Withdraw(decimal amount)
    {
        ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfNegativeOrZero(amount);
        if (amount > Balance) throw new InsufficientFundsException(Balance, amount);
        Balance -= amount;
    }
}
```

With a private setter, the only way to reduce the balance is through `Withdraw`, so the rule
cannot be bypassed.

title: Immutability and encapsulation

## Learning objectives

- Use records and `init` for immutable data
- Model value objects that are always valid
- Protect collections inside aggregates

## Why immutability

Immutable objects are thread-safe, easy to reason about and impossible to corrupt after
construction. In C#, records make them cheap to write:

```csharp
public sealed record Money(decimal Amount, string Currency)
{
    public static Money Zero(string currency) => new(0m, currency);

    public Money Add(Money other) =>
        other.Currency == Currency
            ? this with { Amount = Amount + other.Amount }
            : throw new CurrencyMismatchException(Currency, other.Currency);
}
```

Records provide value-based equality, so `new Money(5, "EUR") == new Money(5, "EUR")` is `true`.

## Always-valid value objects

```csharp
public sealed record EmailAddress
{
    public string Value { get; }

    private EmailAddress(string value) => Value = value;

    public static EmailAddress Parse(string input)
    {
        var trimmed = input?.Trim() ?? throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(input));
        if (!MailAddress.TryCreate(trimmed, out _)) throw new FormatException($"'{input}' is not a valid e-mail address");
        return new EmailAddress(trimmed.ToLowerInvariant());
    }

    public override string ToString() => Value;
}
```

Once you hold an `EmailAddress`, you never need to validate it again. This replaces "primitive
obsession" — passing raw `string`s everywhere and validating them repeatedly.

## Encapsulating collections

```csharp
public sealed class Order
{
    private readonly List<OrderLine> _lines = [];
    public IReadOnlyList<OrderLine> Lines => _lines;

    public void AddLine(Product product, int quantity)
    {
        ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfNegativeOrZero(quantity);
        if (_lines.Count >= 100) throw new OrderTooLargeException();
        _lines.Add(new OrderLine(product.Sku, product.Price, quantity));
    }
}
```

The order controls every change to its lines, so its rules always hold.

## Learning objectives

- Structure tests with Arrange–Act–Assert
- Name tests after behaviour
- Make tests deterministic

## A clean test

```csharp
public class ShoppingCartTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Adding_the_same_product_twice_increases_the_quantity()
    {
        // Arrange
        var cart = new ShoppingCart();
        var book = new Product("SKU-1", 12.50m);

        // Act
        cart.Add(book);
        cart.Add(book);

        // Assert
        var line = Assert.Single(cart.Lines);
        Assert.Equal(2, line.Quantity);
    }
}
```

The name reads as a specification. One behaviour per test, and the assertion checks an observable
outcome.

## FIRST

| Letter | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| Fast | Run in milliseconds so they run constantly |
| Independent | No shared state; any order works |
| Repeatable | Same result on every machine, every time |
| Self-validating | Pass or fail, no manual inspection |
| Timely | Written alongside (or before) the code |

## Controlling time

```csharp
public sealed class TrialService(TimeProvider time)
{
    public bool IsExpired(DateTimeOffset startedAt) => time.GetUtcNow() - startedAt > TimeSpan.FromDays(14);
}

[Fact]
public void Trial_expires_after_fourteen_days()
{
    var time = new FakeTimeProvider(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 1, 15, 0, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));
    var service = new TrialService(time);

    Assert.True(service.IsExpired(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero)));
}
```

`FakeTimeProvider` comes from the `Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing` package and lets
tests control the clock.

## Parameterised tests

```csharp
[Theory]
[InlineData("", false)]
[InlineData("short", false)]
[InlineData("correct-horse-battery", true)]
public void Password_strength(string password, bool expected) =>
    Assert.Equal(expected, PasswordPolicy.IsStrong(password));
```

title: Test-driven development
questions:
  - id: cycle
    prompt: What is the order of the TDD cycle?
    options:

        correct: true

    explanation: Write a failing test (red), make it pass with the simplest code (green), then improve the design with tests as a safety net (refactor).
  - id: doubles
    prompt: What is the difference between a stub and a mock?
    options:
      - id: stub-mock
        text: A stub supplies canned answers; a mock also verifies that expected interactions happened
        correct: true

      - text: Mocks are only used for databases
    explanation: Prefer stubs and fakes for most tests; use mocks when the interaction itself is the behaviour you care about.
  - id: benefits

    type: multiple
    options:

        correct: true
      - text: It forces you to think about the API from the caller's point of view first
        correct: true

## Learning objectives

- Practice the red–green–refactor cycle
- Choose between stubs, fakes and mocks
- Understand what TDD does and does not guarantee

## Red, green, refactor

1. **Red** — write a test for behaviour that does not exist yet; watch it fail
2. **Green** — write the simplest code that makes it pass
3. **Refactor** — clean up duplication and naming with the tests protecting you

```csharp
[Fact]
public void Empty_string_returns_zero() => Assert.Equal(0, StringCalculator.Add(""));
```

```csharp
public static class StringCalculator
{
    public static int Add(string numbers) => 0;
}
```

The next test forces real behaviour:

```csharp
[Theory]
[InlineData("1", 1)]
[InlineData("1,2", 3)]
[InlineData("4,5,6", 15)]
public void Sums_comma_separated_numbers(string input, int expected) =>
    Assert.Equal(expected, StringCalculator.Add(input));
```

```csharp
public static int Add(string numbers) =>
    string.IsNullOrEmpty(numbers) ? 0 : numbers.Split(',').Sum(int.Parse);
```

## Test doubles

| Double | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| Dummy | Fills a parameter, never used |
| Stub | Returns canned answers |
| Fake | A working, simplified implementation (in-memory repository) |
| Spy | Records calls for later assertions |
| Mock | Pre-programmed with expectations it verifies |

Over-mocking couples tests to implementation details. A hand-written fake is often clearer:

```csharp
public sealed class InMemoryOrderRepository : IOrderRepository
{
    private readonly Dictionary<int, Order> _orders = [];
    public Task AddAsync(Order order, CancellationToken ct) { _orders[order.Id] = order; return Task.CompletedTask; }
    public Task<Order?> FindAsync(int id, CancellationToken ct) => Task.FromResult(_orders.GetValueOrDefault(id));
}
```

## What TDD does not do

TDD does not prove correctness, and it does not replace integration tests, exploratory testing or
thinking. It is a design and feedback technique that leaves a useful test suite behind.

title: Common code smells
questions:
  - id: feature-envy
    prompt: "A method in `InvoicePrinter` reads ten properties of `Customer` to compute a discount. Which smell is this?"
    options:
      - text: Long parameter list
      - text: Shotgun surgery
      - text: Dead code
      - id: envy
        text: Feature envy
        correct: true
    explanation: The method is more interested in another class's data than its own. Move the logic to `Customer`.
  - id: shotgun
    prompt: Every time a new currency is supported, you edit eight files in different folders. Which smell is this?
    options:
      - text: Primitive obsession
      - text: Lazy class
      - id: shotgun

        correct: true
    explanation: One conceptual change requires many scattered edits, a sign that the knowledge is not cohesive.
  - id: smell-facts
    prompt: Which statements about code smells are true?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: A smell is a hint that something may be wrong, not proof of a bug
        correct: true
      - text: The term was popularised by Kent Beck and Martin Fowler in "Refactoring"
        correct: true
      - text: Duplicated code is one of the most common smells
        correct: true
      - text: Every smell must be fixed immediately, regardless of context
    explanation: Smells guide attention. Whether to act depends on cost, risk and how often that code changes.
---
## Learning objectives

- Recognise the most common code smells
- Connect each smell to a refactoring

A **code smell** is a surface symptom that often points to a deeper design problem. The catalogue
was popularised by Kent Beck and Martin Fowler in *Refactoring*.

## A field guide

| Smell | Symptom | Typical refactoring |
|-------|---------|---------------------|
| Duplicated code | Same logic in several places | Extract method/class |
| Long method | You scroll to read it | Extract method |
| Large class | Many fields, many responsibilities | Extract class |
| Long parameter list | Many arguments, often primitives | Introduce parameter object |
| Primitive obsession | `string email`, `decimal amount` everywhere | Introduce value object |
| Feature envy | Method uses another class's data more than its own | Move method |
| Shotgun surgery | One change, many files | Move related code together |
| Divergent change | One class changes for many reasons | Extract class (SRP) |
| Switch statements | Same switch duplicated | Replace conditional with polymorphism |
| Speculative generality | Abstractions "for later" | Inline class, remove parameter |
| Dead code | Unused members | Delete |

## Example: primitive obsession

```csharp
public void Transfer(string fromIban, string toIban, decimal amount, string currency) { }
```

```csharp
public void Transfer(Iban from, Iban to, Money amount) { }
```

The second signature cannot be called with arguments in the wrong order, and validation lives in
`Iban` and `Money` once.

## Let tools help

Roslyn analyzers flag many smells automatically — unused members (IDE0051), unused parameters
(IDE0060), and complexity rules such as CA1502 (excessive cyclomatic complexity) when enabled.
Treat analyzer warnings as conversation starters in review, not as noise.

FILE: content/books/clean-code/07-smells-and-refactoring/02-refactoring-safely.md

---
title: Refactoring safely
questions:
  - id: definition
    prompt: How did Martin Fowler define refactoring?
    options:
      - text: Rewriting a system from scratch in a new language
      - text: Adding new features while cleaning up code
      - text: Any change that makes code shorter
      - id: behaviour
        text: Changing the internal structure of code without changing its observable behaviour
        correct: true
    explanation: Refactoring preserves behaviour. Adding features is a separate activity — do not mix them in one step.
  - id: boy-scout
    prompt: What does the Boy Scout Rule say?
    options:
      - text: Never touch code you did not write
      - text: Refactor the whole module before every feature
      - id: cleaner
        text: Leave the code a little cleaner than you found it
        correct: true
    explanation: Small, continuous improvements prevent decay without large, risky rewrites.
  - id: safe-steps
    prompt: Which practices make refactoring safe?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Take small steps and run tests after each one
        correct: true
      - text: Use automated IDE refactorings such as Rename and Extract Method
        correct: true
      - text: Commit refactorings separately from behaviour changes
        correct: true
      - text: Refactor and add a feature in the same large commit to save time
    explanation: Small, tested, separately committed steps keep reviews simple and make it easy to find a mistake.
---
## Learning objectives

- Define refactoring precisely
- Use small, tool-assisted steps
- Make continuous improvement part of daily work

## What refactoring is

> Refactoring: a change made to the internal structure of software to make it easier to understand
> and cheaper to modify without changing its observable behaviour. — Martin Fowler

Kent Beck's "two hats": at any moment you are either adding functionality **or** refactoring.
Switch hats deliberately, never wear both.

## A worked example: replace conditional with polymorphism

```csharp
public decimal Pay(Employee e) => e.Type switch
{
    EmployeeType.Salaried => e.MonthlySalary,
    EmployeeType.Hourly => e.HoursWorked * e.HourlyRate,
    EmployeeType.Commissioned => e.BaseSalary + e.Sales * e.CommissionRate,
    _ => throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(e))
};
```

Steps, running tests after each:

1. Create `abstract class Employee { public abstract decimal Pay(); }`
2. Create one subclass and move its branch into `Pay()`
3. Repeat for each branch
4. Replace the switch with `e.Pay()` and delete the type code

```csharp
public sealed class HourlyEmployee(decimal hours, decimal rate) : Employee
{
    public override decimal Pay() => hours * rate;
}
```

## Use the tools

Visual Studio, Rider and VS Code (C# Dev Kit) provide automated Rename, Extract Method,
Extract Interface, Introduce Parameter and Inline. Automated refactorings are behaviour-preserving
by construction and much faster than manual edits.

## The Boy Scout Rule

Leave the campground cleaner than you found it. Rename one unclear variable, extract one
function, delete one dead method each time you touch a file. Over months this compounds into a
codebase that improves instead of decays — without anyone scheduling a "refactoring sprint".

## Legacy code

Michael Feathers defines legacy code as **code without tests**. To change it safely: find a seam,
write characterisation tests that capture current behaviour, then refactor under their protection.

---
title: What Dapper is and when to use it
questions:
  - id: what
    prompt: What is Dapper?
    options:
      - id: micro-orm
        text: A micro-ORM that adds extension methods to ADO.NET connections for executing SQL and mapping results to objects
        correct: true
      - text: A full ORM with change tracking and migrations
      - text: A database engine
      - text: A replacement for ADO.NET providers such as Microsoft.Data.SqlClient
    explanation: Dapper sits on top of any ADO.NET provider. You write the SQL; Dapper handles parameters and mapping.
  - id: origin
    prompt: Where did Dapper originate?
    options:
      - text: It is part of Entity Framework Core
      - text: It was released by Oracle
      - id: stack-overflow
        text: It was built by the Stack Overflow team to make their data access fast
        correct: true
    explanation: Dapper was created at Stack Overflow and is open source under the Apache 2.0 licence.
  - id: when
    prompt: In which situations is Dapper a particularly good fit?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Read-heavy endpoints where you want precise control over SQL
        correct: true
      - text: Existing databases with complex queries, views or stored procedures
        correct: true
      - text: The read side of a CQRS design, alongside EF Core for writes
        correct: true
      - text: When you want the library to generate and apply schema migrations
    explanation: Dapper has no migrations or change tracking; pair it with a migration tool or EF Core when you need those.
---
## Learning objectives

- Describe what Dapper does and does not do
- Compare Dapper with raw ADO.NET and EF Core
- Decide when Dapper is the right tool

## The problem Dapper solves

Raw ADO.NET is fast but verbose:

```csharp
await using var command = new SqlCommand("SELECT Id, Name, Price FROM Products WHERE Id = @Id", connection);
command.Parameters.AddWithValue("@Id", id);
await using var reader = await command.ExecuteReaderAsync(ct);
Product? product = null;
if (await reader.ReadAsync(ct))
{
    product = new Product
    {
        Id = reader.GetInt32(0),
        Name = reader.GetString(1),
        Price = reader.GetDecimal(2)
    };
}
```

With Dapper:

```csharp
var product = await connection.QuerySingleOrDefaultAsync<Product>(
    "SELECT Id, Name, Price FROM Products WHERE Id = @Id", new { Id = id });
```

Same SQL, same provider, same performance characteristics — without the boilerplate.

## Dapper versus EF Core

| | Dapper | EF Core |
|-|--------|---------|
| You write | SQL | LINQ (SQL generated) |
| Change tracking | No | Yes |
| Migrations | No | Yes |
| Relationships | Manual (multi-mapping) | Navigation properties |
| Overhead | Very low | Low to moderate |
| Learning curve | SQL knowledge | EF concepts + SQL knowledge |

They are not rivals. Many teams use EF Core for writes and aggregates, and Dapper for hot read
paths and reporting queries.

## What Dapper does

- Opens and closes connections when needed
- Converts anonymous objects to command parameters
- Maps result columns to properties or constructor parameters by name
- Caches mapping information so repeated queries are fast

## What it does not do

No change tracking, no identity map, no lazy loading, no LINQ, no schema migrations. You own the
SQL — which is precisely the point.

  - id: open

    options:
      - text: An exception is thrown because the connection is closed
      - id: auto
        text: Dapper opens the connection, runs the query and closes it again
        correct: true
      - text: Dapper creates a second connection
    explanation: Dapper restores the connection's original state. If you open it yourself, it stays open.
  - id: dispose

    options:
      - text: It deletes the database
      - text: Dapper requires it to compile

        correct: true
    explanation: Connections are pooled. Disposing promptly prevents pool exhaustion under load.

## Learning objectives

- Install Dapper and a provider
- Run queries and map results to classes and records
- Manage connection lifetime correctly

## Install

```bash
dotnet add package Dapper
dotnet add package Microsoft.Data.SqlClient   # or Npgsql, MySqlConnector, Microsoft.Data.Sqlite
```

`System.Data.SqlClient` is deprecated; use `Microsoft.Data.SqlClient` for SQL Server.

## A sample table

```sql
CREATE TABLE Products (
    Id INT IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    Name NVARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    Category NVARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    Price DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL,
    CreatedAt DATETIME2 NOT NULL DEFAULT SYSUTCDATETIME()
);
```

## First queries

```csharp
using Dapper;
using Microsoft.Data.SqlClient;

public sealed class Product
{
    public int Id { get; init; }
    public string Name { get; init; } = "";
    public string Category { get; init; } = "";
    public decimal Price { get; init; }
}

await using var connection = new SqlConnection(connectionString);

IEnumerable<Product> books = await connection.QueryAsync<Product>(
    "SELECT Id, Name, Category, Price FROM Products WHERE Category = @Category ORDER BY Name",
    new { Category = "Books" });

int count = await connection.ExecuteScalarAsync<int>("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Products");
```

`@Category` in the SQL matches the `Category` property of the anonymous object. Values are sent as
real parameters, never concatenated into the SQL text.

## Mapping to records

```csharp
public sealed record ProductSummary(int Id, string Name, decimal Price);

var summaries = await connection.QueryAsync<ProductSummary>(
    "SELECT Id, Name, Price FROM Products");
```

For constructor mapping, column names must match the parameter names (case-insensitively) and the
column types must be compatible with the parameter types — for example, a `BIGINT` column will not
map to an `int` parameter. Explicit casts or aliases in SQL fix mismatches.

## Async and cancellation

Use the `...Async` methods in server applications. To pass a cancellation token, use a
`CommandDefinition`:

```csharp
var command = new CommandDefinition(
    "SELECT Id, Name, Price FROM Products WHERE Price > @Min",
    new { Min = 10m },
    cancellationToken: ct);

var expensive = await connection.QueryAsync<ProductSummary>(command);
```

title: Choosing the right query method
questions:
  - id: single-vs-first
    prompt: A query returns two rows. Which method throws an exception?
    options:
      - text: "`QueryFirst`"
      - id: single
        text: "`QuerySingle`"
        correct: true
      - text: "`QueryFirstOrDefault`"
      - text: "`Query`"
    explanation: "`QuerySingle` and `QuerySingleOrDefault` require at most one row (exactly one for `QuerySingle`). The `First` variants take the first row and ignore the rest."
  - id: no-rows
    prompt: A query by primary key returns no rows. Which method returns `null` (for a reference type) without throwing?
    options:
      - text: "`QuerySingle`"
      - id: single-or-default
        text: "`QuerySingleOrDefault`"
        correct: true
      - text: "`QueryFirst`"
    explanation: The `OrDefault` variants return `default(T)` when there are no rows.
  - id: execute
    prompt: Which statements about `Execute` and `ExecuteScalar` are true?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: "`Execute` returns the number of rows affected"
        correct: true
      - text: "`ExecuteScalar<T>` returns the first column of the first row"
        correct: true
      - text: "`Execute` is used for INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements"
        correct: true
      - text: "`ExecuteScalar<T>` returns every row as a list"
    explanation: Use `Query` methods for result sets, `Execute` for commands and `ExecuteScalar` for single values.
---
## Learning objectives

- Pick the query method that matches the expected number of rows
- Use `Execute` and `ExecuteScalar` appropriately

## The family

| Method | 0 rows | 1 row | 2+ rows |
|--------|--------|-------|---------|
| `Query<T>` | Empty | One item | All items |
| `QueryFirst<T>` | Throws | Item | First item |
| `QueryFirstOrDefault<T>` | `default` | Item | First item |
| `QuerySingle<T>` | Throws | Item | Throws |
| `QuerySingleOrDefault<T>` | `default` | Item | Throws |

All have `Async` versions. Choose the one that **expresses your expectation** — the exceptions are
a feature, catching data bugs early.

```csharp
// Exactly one row expected; zero or many is a bug
var order = await db.QuerySingleAsync<Order>("SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Id = @id", new { id });

// Optional lookup
var user = await db.QuerySingleOrDefaultAsync<User>(
    "SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Email = @email", new { email });

// Newest item, possibly none
var latest = await db.QueryFirstOrDefaultAsync<Order>(
    "SELECT TOP (1) * FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId = @customerId ORDER BY CreatedAt DESC",
    new { customerId });
```

When using `First` variants, limit rows in SQL (`TOP (1)`, `LIMIT 1`) so the database does not
send rows you will discard.

## Commands and scalars

```csharp
int affected = await db.ExecuteAsync(
    "UPDATE Products SET Price = Price * 1.05 WHERE Category = @category", new { category });

int newId = await db.ExecuteScalarAsync<int>(
    """
    INSERT INTO Products (Name, Category, Price)
    OUTPUT INSERTED.Id
    VALUES (@Name, @Category, @Price)
    """,
    product);
```

Raw string literals (`"""`) keep multi-line SQL readable. Passing `product` as the parameter object
maps its `Name`, `Category` and `Price` properties to the matching `@` parameters.

## Avoid SELECT * in production

The snippets above use `SELECT *` for brevity. In real code, list columns explicitly: the query
documents its shape, the database does less work, and adding a column to the table cannot break
constructor mapping.

title: Parameters
questions:

        correct: true

    explanation: Matching the parameter type to the column type keeps queries sargable and plans stable.
  - id: injection
    prompt: Which practices prevent SQL injection when using Dapper?
    type: multiple
    options:

        correct: true

        correct: true
      - text: Use string interpolation to insert user input into the SQL text
      - text: Never concatenate untrusted input into SQL
        correct: true
    explanation: Parameters cannot be used for identifiers like column names, so map user choices to known-safe SQL fragments.

## Learning objectives

- Pass parameters with anonymous objects and `DynamicParameters`
- Use list expansion, output parameters and `DbString`
- Keep dynamic SQL safe

## Anonymous objects

```csharp
var results = await db.QueryAsync<Product>(
    "SELECT Id, Name, Price FROM Products WHERE Category = @category AND Price BETWEEN @min AND @max",
    new { category, min = 10m, max = 50m });
```

## Lists

```csharp
int[] ids = [3, 7, 42];
var products = await db.QueryAsync<Product>(
    "SELECT Id, Name, Price FROM Products WHERE Id IN @ids", new { ids });
// Sent as: WHERE Id IN (@ids1, @ids2, @ids3)
```

On PostgreSQL with Npgsql, arrays are native, so the idiomatic form is `WHERE id = ANY(@ids)`.
For very large lists on SQL Server, use a table-valued parameter instead (SQL Server allows at most
2,100 parameters per command).

## DynamicParameters

```csharp
var p = new DynamicParameters();
p.Add("@Name", product.Name);
p.Add("@Price", product.Price, DbType.Decimal, precision: 10, scale: 2);
p.Add("@NewId", dbType: DbType.Int32, direction: ParameterDirection.Output);

await db.ExecuteAsync("dbo.CreateProduct", p, commandType: CommandType.StoredProcedure);
int newId = p.Get<int>("@NewId");
```

`DynamicParameters` is also handy when the set of parameters is built up conditionally.

## Matching string types

```csharp
var order = await db.QuerySingleOrDefaultAsync<Order>(
    "SELECT Id, Code, Total FROM Orders WHERE Code = @code",
    new { code = new DbString { Value = code, IsAnsi = true, Length = 10, IsFixedLength = false } });
```

## Dynamic SQL, safely

```csharp
private static readonly Dictionary<string, string> SortColumns = new(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase)
{
    ["name"] = "Name",
    ["price"] = "Price",
    ["newest"] = "CreatedAt"
};

public Task<IEnumerable<Product>> ListAsync(string sort, bool descending)
{
    var column = SortColumns.GetValueOrDefault(sort, "Name");
    var direction = descending ? "DESC" : "ASC";
    return _db.QueryAsync<Product>($"SELECT Id, Name, Price FROM Products ORDER BY {column} {direction}");
}
```

The interpolated values come only from constants in code, never from the user. Everything the user
supplies goes through parameters.

title: How Dapper maps columns to objects
questions:

        correct: true

  - id: underscores
    prompt: Your PostgreSQL columns use snake_case (`first_name`). What is the simplest way to map them to `FirstName`?
    options:

  - id: unmatched

    type: multiple
    options:

        correct: true
      - text: Dapper throws when any column is not mapped
    explanation: Silent ignoring is convenient but can hide typos — integration tests that assert on mapped values catch them.
  - id: dynamic
    prompt: What does `connection.QueryAsync(sql)` (without a type argument) return?
    options:
      - id: dynamic-rows
        text: "`dynamic` rows whose columns can be accessed as properties or through `IDictionary<string, object>`"
        correct: true
      - text: Raw `DataTable` objects
      - text: JSON strings
    explanation: Dynamic results are handy for ad-hoc scripts and reporting but lose compile-time safety.
---
## Learning objectives

- Understand Dapper's name-matching rules
- Handle naming-convention differences
- Use dynamic results when appropriate

## Name matching

Dapper matches each result column to a settable property, field or constructor parameter with the
same name, ignoring case. Unmatched columns are ignored; unmatched properties keep their defaults.

```csharp
public sealed class Customer
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string FullName { get; set; } = "";
    public string Email { get; set; } = "";
}

var customers = await db.QueryAsync<Customer>(
    """
    SELECT c.Id,
           c.FirstName + ' ' + c.LastName AS FullName,
           c.Email
    FROM Customers c
    """);
```

The alias `AS FullName` maps a computed expression.

## Snake case

```csharp
// once, at startup
Dapper.DefaultTypeMap.MatchNamesWithUnderscores = true;

var people = await db.QueryAsync<Person>("SELECT person_id, first_name, last_name FROM people");
// person_id → PersonId, first_name → FirstName
```

## Custom maps

For full control, register a `CustomPropertyTypeMap`:

```csharp
SqlMapper.SetTypeMap(typeof(LegacyCustomer), new CustomPropertyTypeMap(
    typeof(LegacyCustomer),
    (type, column) => type.GetProperties().FirstOrDefault(p =>
        string.Equals(p.Name, column.Replace("cust_", ""), StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))!));
```

Aliases in SQL are usually clearer than global maps — prefer them unless a whole schema follows a
convention.

## Dynamic results

```csharp
var rows = await db.QueryAsync("SELECT Category, COUNT(*) AS Total FROM Products GROUP BY Category");
foreach (var row in rows)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{row.Category}: {row.Total}");
}
```

Each row is a `DapperRow` that implements `IDictionary<string, object>`. Great for exploration,
but prefer typed results in application code.

## Value tuples

```csharp
var pairs = await db.QueryAsync<(int Id, string Name)>("SELECT Id, Name FROM Products");
```

Tuples map **by position**, not by name — keep the column order aligned with the tuple.

FILE: content/books/dapper/03-advanced-reading/01-multi-mapping.md

---
title: Multi-mapping related objects
questions:
  - id: splaton
    prompt: What does the `splitOn` argument tell Dapper in a multi-mapping query?
    options:
      - text: Which table to join
      - text: How many rows to return
      - text: Which separator character to use for CSV output
      - id: boundary
        text: The column name where the next object's columns begin in each row
        correct: true
    explanation: Dapper reads columns left to right and starts a new object at each `splitOn` column. The default is `Id`.
  - id: one-to-many
    prompt: When multi-mapping a one-to-many join (orders with lines), why do you typically use a dictionary?
    options:
      - text: Dapper requires a dictionary parameter
      - text: To sort the results
      - id: dedupe
        text: Each order appears in several rows, so you look up the existing order and add each line to it
        correct: true
    explanation: The join repeats parent columns for every child row; the dictionary de-duplicates parents.
  - id: limits
    prompt: Which statements about multi-mapping are true?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: The mapping function receives one object per type in the generic argument list
        correct: true
      - text: Dapper supports mapping up to seven input types in one call
        correct: true
      - text: "Columns must be ordered so each object's columns are contiguous"
        correct: true
      - text: Dapper automatically generates the JOIN SQL
    explanation: You write the JOIN; Dapper splits each row into objects and lets you stitch them together.
---
## Learning objectives

- Map one row to several objects with `splitOn`
- Build one-to-many graphs without duplicates
- Know when to use a second query instead

## One-to-one

```csharp
public sealed class Order
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public DateTime PlacedAt { get; set; }
    public Customer Customer { get; set; } = default!;
    public List<OrderLine> Lines { get; } = [];
}

const string sql = """
    SELECT o.Id, o.PlacedAt,
           c.Id, c.FullName, c.Email
    FROM Orders o
    JOIN Customers c ON c.Id = o.CustomerId
    WHERE o.PlacedAt >= @since
    """;

var orders = await db.QueryAsync<Order, Customer, Order>(
    sql,
    (order, customer) => { order.Customer = customer; return order; },
    new { since },
    splitOn: "Id");
```

The second `Id` column starts the `Customer`. If the child's key had a different name, such as
`CustomerId`, you would pass `splitOn: "CustomerId"`; for several splits, a comma-separated list.

## One-to-many

```csharp
const string sql = """
    SELECT o.Id, o.PlacedAt,
           l.Id, l.Sku, l.Quantity, l.UnitPrice
    FROM Orders o
    LEFT JOIN OrderLines l ON l.OrderId = o.Id
    WHERE o.CustomerId = @customerId
    ORDER BY o.Id
    """;

var lookup = new Dictionary<int, Order>();

await db.QueryAsync<Order, OrderLine, Order>(
    sql,
    (order, line) =>
    {
        if (!lookup.TryGetValue(order.Id, out var existing))
        {
            existing = order;
            lookup.Add(order.Id, existing);
        }
        if (line is not null) existing.Lines.Add(line);
        return existing;
    },
    new { customerId },
    splitOn: "Id");

var result = lookup.Values.ToList();
```

With a `LEFT JOIN`, orders without lines produce a row where all line columns are `NULL`. Dapper
passes `null` for that object when the split column is null, hence the null check.

## When to use two queries instead

Joins multiply rows: 100 orders × 20 lines sends 2,000 rows with order columns repeated. For wide
parents or many children, two queries (or `QueryMultiple`, next section) transfer less data.

FILE: content/books/dapper/03-advanced-reading/02-multiple-results-and-procedures.md

---
title: Multiple result sets and stored procedures
questions:
  - id: query-multiple

    options:

      - text: A `DataSet`

    explanation: Result sets must be read in the order the SQL produces them, and the reader must be disposed.
  - id: proc

        correct: true
      - text: Dapper does not support stored procedures
    explanation: With `CommandType.StoredProcedure`, the parameter object's properties become the procedure's parameters.
  - id: benefits

        correct: true

        correct: true

      - text: The batch can share variables and temp tables within one command
        correct: true
    explanation: Fewer round trips and no row multiplication; the price is reading results strictly in order.

## Learning objectives

- Read several result sets in one round trip
- Call stored procedures with input and output parameters

## QueryMultiple

```csharp
const string sql = """
    SELECT Id, CustomerId, PlacedAt, Total FROM Orders WHERE Id = @id;
    SELECT Id, Sku, Quantity, UnitPrice FROM OrderLines WHERE OrderId = @id;
    SELECT Id, Status, ChangedAt FROM OrderHistory WHERE OrderId = @id ORDER BY ChangedAt;
    """;

using var multi = await db.QueryMultipleAsync(sql, new { id });

var order = await multi.ReadSingleOrDefaultAsync<OrderDetails>();
if (order is null) return null;

order.Lines = (await multi.ReadAsync<OrderLine>()).ToList();
order.History = (await multi.ReadAsync<OrderStatusChange>()).ToList();
return order;
```

## Stored procedures

```csharp
var top = await db.QueryAsync<BestSeller>(
    "dbo.GetBestSellers",
    new { Category = "Books", Top = 10 },
    commandType: CommandType.StoredProcedure);
```

With output and return values:

```csharp
var p = new DynamicParameters(new { CustomerId = customerId, Amount = amount });
p.Add("@NewBalance", dbType: DbType.Decimal, direction: ParameterDirection.Output, precision: 18, scale: 2);
p.Add("@Result", dbType: DbType.Int32, direction: ParameterDirection.ReturnValue);

await db.ExecuteAsync("dbo.ApplyCredit", p, commandType: CommandType.StoredProcedure);

var balance = p.Get<decimal>("@NewBalance");
var status = p.Get<int>("@Result");
```

Output parameter values are only available after the command has completed (and, for queries,
after the results have been consumed).

## Table-valued parameters (SQL Server)

```csharp
var table = new DataTable();
table.Columns.Add("Id", typeof(int));
foreach (var id in ids) table.Rows.Add(id);

var rows = await db.QueryAsync<Product>(
    "dbo.GetProductsByIds",
    new { Ids = table.AsTableValuedParameter("dbo.IntList") },
    commandType: CommandType.StoredProcedure);
```

TVPs scale far beyond the 2,100-parameter limit of `IN @list` expansion.

title: Type handlers
questions:
  - id: purpose
    prompt: What is a Dapper type handler for?
    options:
      - text: Handling exceptions thrown by the database
      - text: Choosing which database provider to use
      - id: convert
        text: Converting between a custom .NET type and a database value, in both directions
        correct: true
      - text: Generating SQL from LINQ
    explanation: Implement `SqlMapper.TypeHandler<T>` with `SetValue` (to the database) and `Parse` (from the database).
  - id: register
    prompt: How is a type handler registered?
    options:
      - text: With an attribute on every property
      - text: In the connection string
      - id: add
        text: Once, globally, with `SqlMapper.AddTypeHandler(new MyHandler())` at startup
        correct: true
    explanation: Handlers are global to the process, so register them during application startup.
  - id: uses
    prompt: Which are good uses for type handlers?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Mapping strongly typed IDs such as `record struct OrderId(int Value)`
        correct: true
      - text: Storing a small value object as JSON in a text column
        correct: true
      - text: Mapping a custom `Money` or `EmailAddress` value object to a column
        correct: true
      - text: Replacing SQL joins
    explanation: Type handlers keep domain types in your C# model without manual conversion in every query.
---
## Learning objectives

- Write and register type handlers
- Map strongly typed IDs and JSON columns

## Strongly typed IDs

```csharp
public readonly record struct OrderId(int Value);

public sealed class OrderIdHandler : SqlMapper.TypeHandler<OrderId>
{
    public override void SetValue(IDbDataParameter parameter, OrderId value)
    {
        parameter.DbType = DbType.Int32;
        parameter.Value = value.Value;
    }

    public override OrderId Parse(object value) => new(Convert.ToInt32(value));
}

SqlMapper.AddTypeHandler(new OrderIdHandler());
```

```csharp
public sealed class OrderRow
{
    public OrderId Id { get; init; }
    public DateTime PlacedAt { get; init; }
}

var order = await db.QuerySingleAsync<OrderRow>(
    "SELECT Id, PlacedAt FROM Orders WHERE Id = @id", new { id = new OrderId(42) });
```

Now an `OrderId` cannot be confused with a `CustomerId` anywhere in the codebase.

## JSON columns

```csharp
public sealed record ShippingPreferences(bool LeaveAtDoor, string? Instructions);

public sealed class JsonHandler<T> : SqlMapper.TypeHandler<T?> where T : class
{
    private static readonly JsonSerializerOptions Options = new(JsonSerializerDefaults.Web);

    public override void SetValue(IDbDataParameter parameter, T? value)
    {
        parameter.DbType = DbType.String;
        parameter.Value = value is null ? DBNull.Value : JsonSerializer.Serialize(value, Options);
    }

    public override T? Parse(object value) =>
        value is string json ? JsonSerializer.Deserialize<T>(json, Options) : default;
}

SqlMapper.AddTypeHandler(new JsonHandler<ShippingPreferences>());
```

## Things to know

- Handlers are global; register each one once at startup
- Handlers are used for parameters and for single-column mapping into properties
- Keep `Parse` tolerant of the provider's actual CLR type (for example `long` vs `int`) by using
  `Convert`

title: Inserts, updates and batches
questions:
  - id: enumerable
    prompt: "What does `connection.ExecuteAsync(\"INSERT INTO Tags (Name) VALUES (@Name)\", tags)` do when `tags` is a list of 1,000 objects?"
    options:
      - text: Sends one multi-row INSERT statement
      - text: Throws because a list is not a valid parameter
      - text: Inserts only the first item
      - id: per-item
        text: Executes the command once per item — 1,000 executions
        correct: true
    explanation: Dapper iterates the sequence and executes the command for each element. It is convenient, but it is not a bulk insert.
  - id: bulk
    prompt: For loading 500,000 rows into SQL Server as quickly as possible, which approach is best?
    options:
      - text: "`ExecuteAsync` with a list parameter"
      - id: sqlbulkcopy
        text: "`SqlBulkCopy` (or a provider-specific bulk API such as Npgsql's binary COPY)"
        correct: true
      - text: One `ExecuteAsync` call per row inside a loop with a new connection each time
    explanation: Bulk APIs stream rows using the database's bulk-load protocol and are orders of magnitude faster.
  - id: identity
    prompt: Which are valid ways to get the generated key after an insert on SQL Server?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: "`OUTPUT INSERTED.Id` with `ExecuteScalarAsync<int>`"
        correct: true
      - text: "`SELECT CAST(SCOPE_IDENTITY() AS int)` in the same batch with `ExecuteScalarAsync<int>`"
        correct: true
      - text: "`SELECT MAX(Id) FROM Products` in a separate query"
    explanation: "`MAX(Id)` is wrong under concurrency — another insert can happen in between."
---
## Learning objectives

- Insert and update rows and read generated keys
- Understand how list parameters execute
- Choose bulk APIs for large loads

## Insert and get the key

```csharp
const string insert = """
    INSERT INTO Products (Name, Category, Price)
    OUTPUT INSERTED.Id
    VALUES (@Name, @Category, @Price);
    """;

var id = await db.ExecuteScalarAsync<int>(insert, new { product.Name, product.Category, product.Price });
```

PostgreSQL uses `RETURNING id`; SQLite and others have their own equivalents.

## Update with optimistic concurrency

```csharp
const string update = """
    UPDATE Products
    SET Price = @Price
    WHERE Id = @Id AND RowVersion = @RowVersion;
    """;

var affected = await db.ExecuteAsync(update, new { product.Id, product.Price, product.RowVersion });
if (affected == 0) throw new ConcurrencyException(product.Id);
```

`Execute` returns rows affected, which makes optimistic concurrency checks simple.

## List parameters

```csharp
var tags = new[] { new { Name = "dotnet" }, new { Name = "sql" } };
await db.ExecuteAsync("INSERT INTO Tags (Name) VALUES (@Name)", tags);
```

This runs the INSERT once per element. For a handful of rows inside a transaction it is perfectly
fine; for thousands, use a bulk API.

## Bulk loading

```csharp
using var bulk = new SqlBulkCopy(connection) { DestinationTableName = "dbo.Products", BatchSize = 5_000 };
bulk.ColumnMappings.Add(nameof(Product.Name), "Name");
bulk.ColumnMappings.Add(nameof(Product.Category), "Category");
bulk.ColumnMappings.Add(nameof(Product.Price), "Price");
await bulk.WriteToServerAsync(productsDataTable, ct);
```

`SqlBulkCopy` lives in `Microsoft.Data.SqlClient`. Dapper is not involved — use the right tool.

## Upserts

```sql
-- PostgreSQL
INSERT INTO product_stock (sku, quantity) VALUES (@Sku, @Quantity)
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE SET quantity = EXCLUDED.quantity;
```

On SQL Server, `MERGE` exists but has well-documented concurrency pitfalls; an `UPDATE` followed by
an `INSERT` when no row was affected, inside a transaction with appropriate locking hints, is a
common alternative.

FILE: content/books/dapper/04-writing-data/02-transactions.md

---
title: Transactions
questions:
  - id: pass-tx
    prompt: You start a transaction with `connection.BeginTransaction()`. What must you do on each Dapper call that should participate?
    options:
      - text: Nothing; Dapper detects the transaction automatically
      - id: pass
        text: "Pass the transaction object, for example `transaction: tx`"
        correct: true
      - text: Open a new connection for each call
      - text: Call `tx.Enlist(command)` manually
    explanation: ADO.NET requires each command on that connection to be associated with the active transaction. Forgetting it causes an error.
  - id: open-first
    prompt: Why must the connection be open before calling `BeginTransaction()`?
    options:
      - text: Dapper requires it for logging
      - text: It does not need to be open
      - id: open
        text: A transaction belongs to an open physical connection; ADO.NET cannot begin one on a closed connection
        correct: true
    explanation: Open the connection explicitly, begin the transaction, run commands, then commit.
  - id: facts
    prompt: Which statements about transactions with Dapper are true?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Disposing a transaction that was not committed rolls it back
        correct: true
      - text: Keep transactions short to reduce lock contention
        correct: true
      - text: "`TransactionScope` with `TransactionScopeAsyncFlowOption.Enabled` is needed for async code when using ambient transactions"
        correct: true
      - text: A transaction automatically spans calls made on different connections without any coordination
    explanation: Work across multiple connections requires a distributed transaction, which is best avoided.
---
## Learning objectives

- Run several commands atomically
- Avoid common transaction mistakes
- Encapsulate a unit of work

## Explicit transactions

```csharp
await using var connection = new SqlConnection(connectionString);
await connection.OpenAsync(ct);
await using var tx = await connection.BeginTransactionAsync(ct);

try
{
    var orderId = await connection.ExecuteScalarAsync<int>(
        "INSERT INTO Orders (CustomerId, Total) OUTPUT INSERTED.Id VALUES (@CustomerId, @Total)",
        new { order.CustomerId, order.Total }, tx);

    await connection.ExecuteAsync(
        "INSERT INTO OrderLines (OrderId, Sku, Quantity, UnitPrice) VALUES (@OrderId, @Sku, @Quantity, @UnitPrice)",
        order.Lines.Select(l => new { OrderId = orderId, l.Sku, l.Quantity, l.UnitPrice }), tx);

    await connection.ExecuteAsync(
        "UPDATE Stock SET Quantity = Quantity - @Quantity WHERE Sku = @Sku",
        order.Lines, tx);

    await tx.CommitAsync(ct);
}
catch
{
    await tx.RollbackAsync(ct);
    throw;
}
```

`BeginTransactionAsync` returns a `DbTransaction`; Dapper's `transaction` parameter accepts
`IDbTransaction`, which it implements.

## A unit of work

```csharp
public sealed class UnitOfWork(DbConnection connection) : IAsyncDisposable
{
    private DbTransaction? _tx;
    public DbConnection Connection => connection;
    public DbTransaction Transaction => _tx ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("Call BeginAsync first.");

    public async Task BeginAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        if (connection.State != ConnectionState.Open) await connection.OpenAsync(ct);
        _tx = await connection.BeginTransactionAsync(ct);
    }

    public Task CommitAsync(CancellationToken ct) => Transaction.CommitAsync(ct);

    public async ValueTask DisposeAsync()
    {
        if (_tx is not null) await _tx.DisposeAsync();
        await connection.DisposeAsync();
    }
}
```

Repositories receive the `UnitOfWork` and pass `uow.Transaction` to every call.

## Ambient transactions

```csharp
using var scope = new TransactionScope(TransactionScopeAsyncFlowOption.Enabled);
// open connections and run commands here
scope.Complete();
```

Without `TransactionScopeAsyncFlowOption.Enabled`, the ambient transaction does not flow across
`await`. Opening a second connection inside the scope may escalate to a distributed transaction,
which is not supported everywhere — prefer explicit transactions on one connection.

---
title: Buffering and streaming large results
questions:
  - id: buffered-default
    prompt: By default, what does Dapper's `Query<T>` do with the rows it reads?
    options:
      - id: buffer
        text: Reads them all into a list before returning
        correct: true
      - text: Streams them one at a time while the reader stays open
      - text: Writes them to a temporary file
    explanation: Buffering is the default because it releases the connection quickly and avoids surprises if the caller enumerates slowly.
  - id: unbuffered-async
    prompt: Which method streams rows asynchronously as an `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`?
    options:
      - text: "`QueryMultipleAsync`"
      - text: "`QueryFirstAsync`"
      - text: "`ExecuteReaderAsync`"
      - id: unbuffered
        text: "`QueryUnbufferedAsync`"
        correct: true
    explanation: "`QueryUnbufferedAsync` (on `DbConnection`) yields rows as they arrive, ideal with `await foreach`."
  - id: tradeoffs
    prompt: Which statements about unbuffered queries are true?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Memory use stays flat regardless of the number of rows
        correct: true
      - text: The connection stays busy until enumeration finishes
        correct: true
      - text: You cannot run another command on the same connection while enumerating (without MARS)
        correct: true
      - text: The results can be enumerated twice
    explanation: Streaming trades memory for connection time; the sequence is single-use.
---
## Learning objectives

- Understand buffered versus unbuffered queries
- Stream large result sets with `QueryUnbufferedAsync`

## Buffered by default

```csharp
var all = await db.QueryAsync<Product>("SELECT Id, Name, Price FROM Products");
// all rows are already in memory here
```

Great for typical result sizes: the reader is closed and the connection released immediately.

## Streaming

```csharp
await using var connection = new SqlConnection(connectionString);

await foreach (var row in connection.QueryUnbufferedAsync<AuditRow>(
    "SELECT Id, At, UserId, Action FROM AuditLog WHERE At >= @since", new { since }))
{
    await writer.WriteLineAsync($"{row.At:O},{row.UserId},{row.Action}");
}
```

Memory stays flat even for millions of rows — useful for exports and ETL jobs.

The synchronous API also supports streaming with `buffered: false`:

```csharp
foreach (var row in connection.Query<AuditRow>(sql, param, buffered: false)) { /* ... */ }
```

## Streaming to an HTTP response

```csharp
app.MapGet("/export/audit", (DbConnection db, DateTime since) =>
    db.QueryUnbufferedAsync<AuditRow>("SELECT Id, At, UserId, Action FROM AuditLog WHERE At >= @since", new { since }));
```

This assumes a scoped `DbConnection` registration (see the next chapter). Returning `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` from a minimal API endpoint streams a JSON array to the client as
rows are read, without collecting them first.

## Rules of thumb

| Situation | Choose |
|-----------|--------|
| Up to a few thousand rows | Buffered (default) |
| Exports, reports, ETL with large volumes | Unbuffered/streaming |
| Need to run more commands while iterating | Buffered, or a second connection |

## Learning objectives

- Create connections through an abstraction
- Register data access correctly in DI
- Use `DbDataSource` where available

## A small factory

```csharp
public interface IDbConnectionFactory
{
    Task<DbConnection> OpenAsync(CancellationToken ct = default);
}

public sealed class SqlConnectionFactory(IOptions<DatabaseOptions> options) : IDbConnectionFactory
{
    public async Task<DbConnection> OpenAsync(CancellationToken ct = default)
    {
        var connection = new SqlConnection(options.Value.ConnectionString);
        await connection.OpenAsync(ct);
        return connection;
    }
}

builder.Services.AddOptions<DatabaseOptions>().BindConfiguration("Database").ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart();
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IDbConnectionFactory, SqlConnectionFactory>();
```

## DbDataSource

.NET 7 introduced `System.Data.Common.DbDataSource`. Npgsql implements it fully:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddNpgsqlDataSource(builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Shop")!);

public sealed class ProductQueries(NpgsqlDataSource dataSource)
{
    public async Task<IReadOnlyList<ProductSummary>> ListAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await using var connection = await dataSource.OpenConnectionAsync(ct);
        var rows = await connection.QueryAsync<ProductSummary>(
            new CommandDefinition("SELECT id, name, price FROM products ORDER BY name", cancellationToken: ct));
        return rows.AsList();
    }
}
```

`AddNpgsqlDataSource` comes from the `Npgsql.DependencyInjection` package. `AsList()` is a Dapper
helper that avoids copying when the result is already a `List<T>`.

## Lifetimes

| Thing | Lifetime |
|-------|----------|
| Connection factory / data source | Singleton |
| Repositories / query services (stateless) | Singleton or scoped |
| Connections | Per operation or per unit of work — always disposed |
| Transactions | Per unit of work |

## Identity-based connections

In the cloud, prefer passwordless authentication — for example `Authentication=Active Directory Default`
in an Azure SQL connection string with a managed identity — so no secret appears in configuration at all.

title: Repositories, query objects and CQRS
questions:

    prompt: A read-only dashboard needs three queries. Which design follows the Interface Segregation Principle?
    options:

## Learning objectives

- Design query and command interfaces around use cases
- Apply SOLID to a Dapper data layer
- Keep SQL organised and testable

## Use-case-shaped interfaces

```csharp
public interface IOrderQueries
{
    Task<OrderDetails?> GetDetailsAsync(int orderId, CancellationToken ct);
    Task<IReadOnlyList<OrderSummary>> ListRecentAsync(int customerId, int take, CancellationToken ct);
}

public interface IOrderCommands
{
    Task<int> PlaceAsync(PlaceOrder command, CancellationToken ct);
    Task CancelAsync(int orderId, CancellationToken ct);
}
```

## An implementation

```csharp
public sealed class SqlOrderQueries(IDbConnectionFactory connections) : IOrderQueries
{
    private const string RecentSql = """
        SELECT TOP (@take) o.Id, o.PlacedAt, o.Total, o.Status
        FROM Orders o
        WHERE o.CustomerId = @customerId
        ORDER BY o.PlacedAt DESC
        """;

    public async Task<IReadOnlyList<OrderSummary>> ListRecentAsync(int customerId, int take, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await using var db = await connections.OpenAsync(ct);
        var rows = await db.QueryAsync<OrderSummary>(new CommandDefinition(RecentSql, new { customerId, take }, cancellationToken: ct));
        return rows.AsList();
    }

    public async Task<OrderDetails?> GetDetailsAsync(int orderId, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await using var db = await connections.OpenAsync(ct);
        using var multi = await db.QueryMultipleAsync(new CommandDefinition(DetailsSql, new { orderId }, cancellationToken: ct));
        var order = await multi.ReadSingleOrDefaultAsync<OrderDetails>();
        if (order is not null) order.Lines = (await multi.ReadAsync<OrderLine>()).AsList();
        return order;
    }

    private const string DetailsSql = """
        SELECT Id, CustomerId, PlacedAt, Total, Status FROM Orders WHERE Id = @orderId;
        SELECT Sku, Quantity, UnitPrice FROM OrderLines WHERE OrderId = @orderId;
        """;
}
```

## SOLID applied

| Principle | In this design |
|-----------|----------------|
| SRP | Queries and commands live in separate classes |
| OCP | New use cases add methods or classes; existing SQL is untouched |
| LSP | Any `IOrderQueries` (SQL, cached decorator, fake) behaves the same to callers |
| ISP | Consumers depend on `IOrderQueries` or `IOrderCommands`, not both |
| DIP | Application code depends on the interfaces; only the composition root knows about SQL |

## A caching decorator

```csharp
public sealed class CachedOrderQueries(IOrderQueries inner, HybridCache cache) : IOrderQueries
{
    public async Task<OrderDetails?> GetDetailsAsync(int orderId, CancellationToken ct) =>
        await cache.GetOrCreateAsync($"order:{orderId}", async t => await inner.GetDetailsAsync(orderId, t), cancellationToken: ct);

    public Task<IReadOnlyList<OrderSummary>> ListRecentAsync(int customerId, int take, CancellationToken ct) =>
        inner.ListRecentAsync(customerId, take, ct);
}
```

title: Security and performance
questions:
  - id: interpolation
    prompt: "Is `db.QueryAsync<User>($\"SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Name = '{name}'\")` safe if `name` comes from a query string?"
    options:
      - text: Yes, Dapper escapes interpolated strings automatically
      - id: unsafe
        text: No — the value is concatenated into the SQL text, which allows SQL injection
        correct: true
      - text: Yes, as long as the column is indexed
    explanation: Dapper only protects values passed as parameters. Plain string interpolation produces a raw SQL string.
  - id: least-privilege
    prompt: Which database permission setup follows the principle of least privilege for a typical web app?
    options:
      - id: least
        text: An application login that can only read and write the tables (or execute the procedures) it needs
        correct: true
      - text: The `sa` or database owner account, for simplicity
      - text: A shared admin account used by every service
    explanation: Limited permissions contain the damage of a compromised application or an injection bug.
  - id: perf
    prompt: Which practices improve the performance of Dapper-based data access?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Select only the columns you need
        correct: true
      - text: Keep SQL text stable and parameterised so the database can reuse execution plans
        correct: true
      - text: Match parameter types to column types (for example `DbString` with `IsAnsi` for `VARCHAR`)
        correct: true
      - text: Open a new connection for every row in a loop
    explanation: Fewer bytes, reused plans and sargable predicates matter far more than micro-optimising C#.
  - id: aot
    prompt: What does Dapper.AOT add?
    options:
      - text: Automatic migrations
      - id: source-gen
        text: A source generator that produces the mapping code at build time, avoiding runtime reflection and supporting Native AOT
        correct: true
      - text: A LINQ provider
    explanation: Dapper.AOT uses C# interceptors to replace calls to Dapper's methods with generated code.
---
## Learning objectives

- Prevent SQL injection
- Apply least privilege
- Tune Dapper queries for performance

## SQL injection

```csharp
// Vulnerable
await db.QueryAsync<User>($"SELECT Id, Name FROM Users WHERE Name = '{name}'");

// Safe
await db.QueryAsync<User>("SELECT Id, Name FROM Users WHERE Name = @name", new { name });
```

An attacker sending `' OR 1=1 --` as the name dumps the table in the first version. Analyzers and
code review should flag any SQL built with interpolation of non-constant values.

## Least privilege

```sql
CREATE USER shop_app FOR LOGIN shop_app;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE ON SCHEMA::sales TO shop_app;
GRANT EXECUTE ON OBJECT::sales.PlaceOrder TO shop_app;
```

The application cannot drop tables or read other schemas, even if compromised.

## Performance checklist

- **Columns** — list them; avoid `SELECT *`
- **Parameters** — never inline values; stable SQL text means plan reuse
- **Types** — match `NVARCHAR` vs `VARCHAR`, `DECIMAL` precision, `DATETIME2`
- **Round trips** — use `QueryMultiple` or joins instead of N+1 loops
- **Paging** — use `OFFSET ... FETCH` or keyset pagination (`WHERE Id > @lastId`) for deep pages
- **Indexes** — check actual execution plans for scans on hot queries

## Keyset pagination

```csharp
const string sql = """
    SELECT TOP (@pageSize) Id, Name, Price
    FROM Products
    WHERE Id > @afterId
    ORDER BY Id
    """;
var page = await db.QueryAsync<ProductSummary>(sql, new { afterId, pageSize = 50 });
```

Unlike `OFFSET`, keyset paging stays fast however deep the user goes.

## Dapper.AOT

```xml
<PackageReference Include="Dapper.AOT" />
<PropertyGroup>
  <InterceptorsNamespaces>$(InterceptorsNamespaces);Dapper.AOT</InterceptorsNamespaces>
</PropertyGroup>
```

```csharp
[module: DapperAot]
```

Your Dapper calls stay the same; the generator emits strongly typed code for parameters and
mapping at build time, which suits Native AOT and trimmed apps.

## Learning objectives

- Test SQL against a real database engine
- Keep integration tests isolated and fast
- Test consumers of the data layer with fakes

## Two kinds of tests

| What | How |
|------|-----|
| Query/command classes (the SQL) | Integration tests against a real engine |
| Services that use `IOrderQueries` | Unit tests with a fake implementation |

Thanks to the interfaces from the previous section, business logic never needs a database to be tested.

## A database fixture

```csharp
public sealed class DatabaseFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly MsSqlContainer _sql = new MsSqlBuilder()
        .WithImage("mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2022-latest")
        .Build();

    public IDbConnectionFactory Connections { get; private set; } = default!;

    public async ValueTask InitializeAsync()
    {
        await _sql.StartAsync();
        var connectionString = _sql.GetConnectionString();
        await SchemaMigrator.ApplyAsync(connectionString);   // e.g. DbUp, EF migrations bundle, or SQL scripts
        Connections = new TestConnectionFactory(connectionString);
    }

    public async ValueTask DisposeAsync() => await _sql.DisposeAsync();
}
```

## A query test

```csharp
public sealed class SqlOrderQueriesTests(DatabaseFixture db) : IClassFixture<DatabaseFixture>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task ListRecent_returns_newest_first_and_respects_take()
    {
        var ct = TestContext.Current.CancellationToken;
        var customerId = await TestData.CustomerWithOrdersAsync(db.Connections,
            placedAt: [new DateTime(2026, 1, 1), new DateTime(2026, 3, 1), new DateTime(2026, 2, 1)], ct);

        var orders = await new SqlOrderQueries(db.Connections).ListRecentAsync(customerId, take: 2, ct);

        Assert.Equal(new[] { new DateTime(2026, 3, 1), new DateTime(2026, 2, 1) }, orders.Select(o => o.PlacedAt));
    }
}
```

Each test creates its own customer, so tests do not interfere with each other even when they share
a database.

## Fakes for consumers

```csharp
public sealed class FakeOrderQueries(params OrderSummary[] orders) : IOrderQueries
{
    public Task<IReadOnlyList<OrderSummary>> ListRecentAsync(int customerId, int take, CancellationToken ct) =>
        Task.FromResult<IReadOnlyList<OrderSummary>>(orders.Take(take).ToList());

    public Task<OrderDetails?> GetDetailsAsync(int orderId, CancellationToken ct) =>
        Task.FromResult<OrderDetails?>(null);
}
```

## Learning objectives

- Explain the lakehouse architecture and its motivation
- Identify the open-source projects at the heart of Databricks
- Describe the main workloads the platform supports

## From warehouses and lakes to lakehouses

| Generation | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|------------|-----------|------------|
| Data warehouse | Fast SQL, transactions, governance | Expensive, proprietary formats, poor for unstructured data and ML |
| Data lake | Cheap, open files, any data type | No transactions, "data swamp", weak governance |
| Two-tier (lake + warehouse) | Combines both | Duplicate data, complex ETL, staleness |
| **Lakehouse** | Warehouse features on open lake storage | Requires a capable table format and engine |

The enabling technology is an **open table format** — Delta Lake on Databricks, with Apache
Iceberg interoperability — that adds a transaction log on top of Parquet files.

## The Databricks Data Intelligence Platform

Databricks was founded in 2013 by the creators of Apache Spark. Its platform runs on AWS, Azure
and Google Cloud and is built from open-source foundations:

| Project | Role |
|---------|------|
| Apache Spark | Distributed processing engine |
| Delta Lake | ACID table format on object storage |
| MLflow | Machine learning lifecycle and GenAI evaluation |
| Unity Catalog (open-sourced in 2024) | Governance for data and AI assets |
| Delta Sharing | Open protocol for sharing data |

## Workloads on one platform

- **Data engineering** — batch and streaming pipelines (Lakeflow)
- **Data warehousing and BI** — Databricks SQL, AI/BI dashboards, Genie
- **Data science and ML** — notebooks, MLflow, Model Serving
- **Generative AI** — vector search, foundation model APIs, agents
- **Governance** — Unity Catalog across all of the above

> Databricks renames products often. This book uses current names and mentions earlier names where
> you are likely to meet them in documentation and existing code.

## Learning objectives

- Distinguish the control plane from the compute plane
- Understand accounts, workspaces and metastores
- Know where your data actually lives

## Two planes

```text
┌──────────────── Control plane (Databricks-managed) ────────────────┐
│  Web UI · Notebooks · Jobs scheduler · Cluster manager · Unity Catalog │
└───────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                                │
     ┌──────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┐
     │                                                     │
Classic compute plane                              Serverless compute plane
(your cloud account)                               (managed by Databricks)
  clusters, SQL warehouses                           serverless notebooks, jobs,
                                                     SQL warehouses, pipelines
     │                                                     │
     └─────────────── Your cloud object storage ───────────┘
                    (S3 · ADLS Gen2 · GCS)
```

Your table data stays in **your** object storage. Compute reads and writes it; the control plane
orchestrates.

## Accounts, workspaces and metastores

| Concept | Scope | Purpose |
|---------|-------|---------|
| Account | Organisation | Identity (users, groups, service principals), billing, metastores |
| Workspace | Deployment | Notebooks, jobs, compute, dashboards — a place where teams work |
| Metastore | Region | Top-level Unity Catalog container, attached to workspaces in that region |

A common pattern is separate workspaces for development, staging and production, all attached to
the same regional metastore, with catalogs per environment (`dev`, `prod`) controlling access.

## Identities

- **Users** — people, usually synced from an identity provider via SCIM
- **Groups** — the unit you grant privileges to
- **Service principals** — identities for jobs and CI/CD pipelines

Grant privileges to groups, not individuals, and run production jobs as service principals.

## Notebooks

Notebooks combine code, results, visualisations and Markdown. A notebook has a default language
(Python, SQL, Scala or R), and individual cells can switch with magic commands:

```python
df = spark.read.table("samples.nyctaxi.trips")
display(df.limit(10))
```

```sql
%sql
SELECT pickup_zip, COUNT(*) AS trips
FROM samples.nyctaxi.trips
GROUP BY pickup_zip
ORDER BY trips DESC
LIMIT 10
```

`spark` (a `SparkSession`) and `display()` are available automatically.

## Magic commands

| Command | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| `%sql`, `%python`, `%scala`, `%r` | Change cell language |
| `%md` | Markdown documentation |
| `%pip install pkg` | Install a notebook-scoped Python library |
| `%run ./helpers` | Run another notebook inline |
| `%sh` | Shell commands on the driver |

## Widgets as parameters

```python
dbutils.widgets.text("run_date", "2026-11-01", "Run date")
run_date = dbutils.widgets.get("run_date")

orders = spark.read.table("prod.sales.orders").where(f"order_date = '{run_date}'")
```

When the notebook runs as a job task, job parameters populate the widgets. (For SQL, prefer
parameter markers such as `:run_date` over string formatting.)

## Secrets

```python
password = dbutils.secrets.get(scope="erp", key="jdbc-password")

```

## Files

```python
display(dbutils.fs.ls("/Volumes/main/raw/landing/"))
```

Unity Catalog **volumes** (`/Volumes/<catalog>/<schema>/<volume>/...`) are the governed place for
non-tabular files. The legacy DBFS root is discouraged for new work.

## Beyond notebooks

Notebooks are great for exploration. For production code, move logic into Python modules or
packages in Git folders, add unit tests, and call them from thin notebooks or Python script tasks.

---
title: How Spark executes work
questions:
  - id: lazy
    prompt: "What happens when you run `df2 = df.filter(df.amount > 100).select(\"id\")` in PySpark?"
    options:
      - id: plan
        text: Nothing is computed yet; Spark records the transformations in a logical plan
        correct: true
      - text: Spark immediately reads the data and filters it
      - text: The data is copied to the driver
      - text: Spark writes a temporary table
    explanation: Transformations are lazy. Work only happens when an action such as `count()`, `show()`, `collect()` or a write is called.
  - id: wide
    prompt: Which operation causes a shuffle?
    options:
      - id: groupby
        text: "`groupBy(...).agg(...)`"
        correct: true
      - text: "`filter`"
      - text: "`select`"
      - text: "`withColumn`"
    explanation: Wide transformations such as aggregations, joins (other than broadcast joins) and `repartition` move data between executors across the network.
  - id: roles
    prompt: Which statements about Spark's architecture are true?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: The driver builds the execution plan and schedules tasks
        correct: true
      - text: Executors run tasks, each task processing one partition
        correct: true
      - text: A job is split into stages at shuffle boundaries
        correct: true
      - text: "`collect()` on a huge DataFrame is safe because data stays on the executors"
    explanation: "`collect()` brings every row to the driver and can exhaust its memory."
---
## Learning objectives

- Describe the driver, executors, jobs, stages and tasks
- Distinguish transformations from actions
- Recognise narrow and wide transformations

## Architecture

| Component | Role |
|-----------|------|
| Driver | Runs your program, builds the plan, schedules tasks |
| Executors | JVM processes on worker nodes that run tasks and cache data |
| Partition | A chunk of data processed by one task |
| Job | Triggered by an action |
| Stage | A set of tasks that can run without a shuffle |
| Task | Unit of work on one partition |

## Lazy evaluation

```python
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

trips = spark.read.table("samples.nyctaxi.trips")              # transformation
long_trips = trips.where(F.col("trip_distance") > 10)          # transformation
by_zip = long_trips.groupBy("pickup_zip").agg(F.avg("fare_amount").alias("avg_fare"))  # transformation

by_zip.show(5)                                                 # action → job runs
```

Laziness lets Spark's **Catalyst** optimiser rewrite the whole plan: pushing filters down to the
file scan, pruning unused columns and choosing join strategies.

```python
by_zip.explain(mode="formatted")
```

## Narrow vs wide

| Narrow (no shuffle) | Wide (shuffle) |
|---------------------|----------------|
| `select`, `where`, `withColumn`, `union` | `groupBy`, `join`, `distinct`, `orderBy`, `repartition` |

Shuffles write data to disk and send it over the network, so they dominate the cost of most jobs.
Each shuffle boundary starts a new stage.

## Actions to be careful with

- `collect()` / `toPandas()` — pull all data to the driver; only for small results
- `count()` on huge tables just to log a number — it triggers a full job
- Repeated actions on the same expensive DataFrame — consider caching or writing an intermediate table

- Transform data with the DataFrame API
- Write equivalent logic in Spark SQL

## Reading and writing

```python
orders = spark.read.table("main.sales.orders")

raw = (spark.read
       .format("json")
       .option("multiLine", "true")
       .load("/Volumes/main/raw/landing/orders/"))

(orders.write
       .mode("overwrite")
       .saveAsTable("main.sales.orders_snapshot"))
```

On Databricks, `saveAsTable` creates a Delta table by default.

## Transformations

```python
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

daily = (orders
    .where(F.col("status") == "COMPLETED")
    .withColumn("order_date", F.to_date("ordered_at"))
    .groupBy("order_date", "country")
    .agg(F.sum("total").alias("revenue"), F.countDistinct("customer_id").alias("customers")))

w = Window.partitionBy("country").orderBy("order_date")
with_growth = daily.withColumn("prev_revenue", F.lag("revenue").over(w))
```

## The same in SQL

```sql
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT to_date(ordered_at) AS order_date, country,
         SUM(total) AS revenue, COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customers
  FROM main.sales.orders
  WHERE status = 'COMPLETED'
  GROUP BY ALL
)
SELECT *, LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY order_date) AS prev_revenue
FROM daily;
```

`GROUP BY ALL` groups by every non-aggregated column in the select list.

## Mixing the two

```python
daily.createOrReplaceTempView("daily")
top = spark.sql("SELECT * FROM daily WHERE revenue > :min", args={"min": 10000})
```

Named parameter markers (`:min` with `args=`) avoid SQL injection and string formatting bugs.

## UDFs

```python
import pandas as pd
from pyspark.sql.functions import pandas_udf

@pandas_udf("double")
def to_celsius(f: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    return (f - 32) * 5 / 9

readings.withColumn("temp_c", to_celsius("temp_f"))
```

Better yet, here a built-in expression — `(F.col("temp_f") - 32) * 5 / 9` — does the job with no
UDF at all.

title: Spark performance fundamentals
questions:
  - id: broadcast
    prompt: Joining a 2 TB fact table with a 5 MB dimension table, which join strategy is usually best?
    options:
      - text: Sort-merge join, shuffling both tables
      - id: broadcast
        text: Broadcast hash join, sending the small table to every executor
        correct: true
      - text: Cartesian join
      - text: Collect both tables to the driver
    explanation: Broadcasting the small side avoids shuffling the large table. Spark does this automatically below `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` (10 MB by default), and AQE can switch to it at runtime.
  - id: aqe
    prompt: What does Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) do?
    options:
      - text: Automatically adds indexes to tables
      - text: Rewrites Python code into Scala
      - id: runtime
        text: Re-optimises the query plan at runtime using statistics from completed stages, for example coalescing shuffle partitions and handling skewed joins
        correct: true
    explanation: AQE is enabled by default in modern Spark and Databricks Runtime.
  - id: small-files
    prompt: Which are common causes of slow Spark jobs?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Data skew, where a few partitions are much larger than the rest
        correct: true
      - text: Many tiny files, which add per-file overhead
        correct: true
      - text: Unnecessary shuffles and wide transformations
        correct: true
      - text: Using Delta Lake instead of CSV
    explanation: Skew, small files and shuffles dominate. Delta Lake usually improves performance through data skipping and compaction.
---
## Learning objectives

- Read the Spark UI to find bottlenecks
- Choose join strategies and handle skew
- Know when caching helps

## Where time goes

Use the **Spark UI** (or the query profile in Databricks SQL) to find:

- Stages with the most time and shuffle read/write
- Tasks much slower than the median — a sign of **skew**
- Spill to disk — partitions too large for executor memory

## Joins

```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast

enriched = sales.join(broadcast(stores), "store_id")
```

| Strategy | When |
|----------|------|
| Broadcast hash join | One side is small |
| Sort-merge join | Both sides large |
| Shuffle hash join | Medium, unsorted sides (AQE may choose it) |

## Adaptive Query Execution

AQE (on by default) uses runtime statistics to:

- Coalesce many small shuffle partitions into fewer, right-sized ones
- Convert sort-merge joins to broadcast joins when one side turns out small
- Split skewed partitions in joins

## Partitions and files

- `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` defaults to 200; AQE adjusts it at runtime
- Avoid writing thousands of tiny files: compact Delta tables with `OPTIMIZE` or enable
  auto-optimise / predictive optimization (see the Delta chapter)
- Filter on clustering or partition columns so Delta can skip files

## Caching

```python
features = spark.read.table("main.ml.features").where("country = 'DE'").cache()
features.count()   # materialise
```

Cache only when the same DataFrame is reused several times in one job. On Databricks, the
**disk cache** automatically caches remote Parquet/Delta data on local SSDs for repeated reads.

## Photon

Photon is Databricks' vectorised query engine written in C++. It accelerates SQL and DataFrame
operations without code changes and is enabled by default on SQL warehouses and serverless compute.
